### Bandarpur

# Bandarpur

Bandarpur is a single **megacity-state** spanning the real-world Adam's Bridge (Rama Setu) shoal chain between Pamban Island (India) and Mannar Island (Sri Lanka). It is organised as two extreme-density land endcaps anchoring a segmented inhabited spine along the shoals, with twelve circular harbour boroughs set off the spine. The system is designed to read clearly on a top-down map, to be architecturally distinctive through ring-vestibule urbanism, and to be operationally credible through night-hardening and protected underwater layers. Its primary power is tidal/hydro, and it is Dharti's major port and logistics hub.

## Governance and identity

Bandarpur operates as one megacity-state entity with unified administration, infrastructure planning, and a single census frame across the endcaps, spine, and harbour boroughs.

## Population and allocation (75 million total)

| Component | Resident population |
| --- | --- |
| West endcap (India side) | 22 million (incl. West Mega Tower: 2.5 million) |
| East endcap (Sri Lanka side) | 18 million (incl. East Mega Tower: 2.0 million) |
| Adam's Bridge inhabited spine | 11 million |
| Off-spine circular harbour boroughs (12 total) | 23 million combined |
| Minor satellites and service settlements | 1 million |
| **Total** | **75 million** |

## Geography baseline

The map basis is the current real geography of Adam's Bridge (Rama Setu), including the shoal chain between Dhanushkodi (Pamban Island) and Talaimannar (Mannar Island), with the Palk Strait to the north and the Gulf of Mannar to the south.

## Underwater build share

About **25%** of total citywide floor area is below the waterline. In the harbour boroughs, **30%** of borough floor area is below the waterline; of that underwater floor area, **60% is habitable** and **40%** is utilities, freight, ballast, and water systems. The underwater layer is core to both the city's visual identity and its night-safe operations, using compartmentalisation, protected circulation, and light-well systems.

## Spatial layout

- **West endcap (India side):** extreme-density land city with one residential mega tower.
- **East endcap (Sri Lanka side):** extreme-density land city with one residential mega tower.
- **Adam's Bridge spine:** a segmented inhabited chain aligned to the shoals, with gaps over open water.
- **Off-spine harbours:** 12 circular harbour boroughs, alternating north and south of the spine.

### Tidal throats (navigation and energy gates)

- **Jaya Gate** — primary tidal throat and navigation control point.
- **Vijaya Gate** — secondary tidal throat and navigation control point.

Both gates appear on the map as deep navigation channels crossing the shoal chain, paired with gateworks infrastructure and managed shipping corridors.

## Harbour borough system

**Standard harbour anatomy:** an inhabited outer breakwater ring (powerworks, sluice grilles, maintenance gantries, controlled access); a calmer inner-lagoon commons (civic decks, markets, water-transport lanes); 2–4 radial causeway/service spokes connecting to the spine (not rail); and a continuous below-water hull layer (the 30% underwater rule).

**Size classes:** S (6–7 km diameter, ~0.9 M each, 3 total); M (8–9 km, ~1.6 M each, 3 total); L (10–11 km, ~2.2 M each, 3 total); XL (12–14 km, ~3.0 M each, 3 total).

**Hero harbours (story focus):** one per size class — Muthu Mandala (S), Kaveri Bazaar Mandala (M), Varuna Sabha Mandala (L), and Jaya Gateworks Mandala (XL).

**Canonical harbour register:**

| Harbour borough | Class | Diameter (km) | Hero | Primary role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Muthu Mandala (Pearl Circle) | S | 6.6 | Hero | Reef craft, jewellery materials, specialty aquaculture |
| Kaveri Bazaar Mandala (River Market Circle) | M | 8.7 | Hero | Markets, food distribution, education, clinics |

| Kelp Crown Mandala (Laminar Belt Circle) | M | 8.1 | — | Aquaculture belt management, processing, logistics support |

## Underwater urbanism

Within harbour boroughs the underwater layer divides into **Hull Districts** (habitable: compact residential/civic blocks around light wells and sealed transfer lobbies), **Vault Corridors** (protected below-water movement and commerce corridors that stay operational in rough weather and night protocols), and **Plant & Ballast** (non-habitable: water treatment, waste processing, freight handling, buoyancy control, maintenance access).

## Transport

Bandarpur uses the Hovercraft-Maglev Freight System: maglev infrastructure is restricted to land and island segments, and across open-water gaps vehicles transition to hovercraft operation along designated hover corridors. Network layers comprise land metros and endcap interchanges; shoal/island maglev guideways; dashed-route marine hover corridors; and harbour access causeways/spokes (no rail symbols across water). Operational constraints: stations and major public buildings use nested ring vestibules that seal progressively as hazard rises; hover legs slow or suspend in rough seas, with protected submerged approaches preferred near gateworks; freight concentrates in protected night windows, especially in XL gateworks harbours.

## Architectural identity

Recurring motifs: **the Rings** (ring vestibules and circular thresholds across stations, markets, and civic buildings); **the Throats** (heavy, infrastructurally loud gateworks with turbine galleries and controlled navigation apertures); and **the Waterline Band** (consistent below-water glazing and intake grilles marking the underwater hull). Most districts are low-rise (2–10 storeys) with vertical punctuation at interchanges. Each endcap holds one **mega tower** — a stepped arcology with multiple cores, stacked neighbourhood plates, and sealed transfer lobbies integrated with transit.

## Narrative role (Arc 2)

Bandarpur is the focus of Arc 2. The team comes to consult insect specialists because the nocturnal insects are becoming more resilient to resin smoke; meanwhile the city was built on and in the water to keep distance from the insects, so as ocean levels recede that natural protection weakens and tsunami risk rises. The arc's twist is that the Khanna Microfoundry Group is **not lying** about the danger — its warnings are materially correct — but it uses that truth to push an expansionist agenda. Movement through Bandarpur also gives Indu another traceable clue to Echo's location. (See `arc-2`.)

### Mara
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Mara

Mara is a highland megacity embedded into the sides of Mt Kenya, lit and ventilated from a single summit megastructure, the Crown Lantern. Its primary power is biomass transitioning to nuclear, and that nuclear transition is the most destabilising development on Dharti: surplus energy is otherwise rare and politically meaningful, so Mara's energy advantage upends the long-standing equilibrium between cities and makes Mara a geopolitical outlier rather than simply prosperous.

## Crown Lantern

Mara's signature system is the Crown Lantern, a summit megastructure that provides citywide light distribution and hosts the primary controlled air-exchange headworks. All illumination delivered through the city's lightwell network originates at the Crown Lantern (the singular-origin rule). Full technical detail — light sourcing and conditioning, the eight sealed Light Spines, the equity rule, the circadian sky-cycle, and the safety modes — lives in the Crown Lantern Lightwell System entry. It is maintained by the Lanternwrights.

## Expansion and disruption

Mara's energy advantage enables expansionist projects that destabilise Dharti's norms. It begins establishing the first new city in centuries; it launches the first man-made satellites (global observation and telecom beyond the ring network); and it introduces early weapons and tactics that are culturally shocking in a civilisation without militaries. Mara starts as a central consolidated authority and, as it becomes expansionist, grants regional leadership to newly established cities aligned to its strategic objectives. In Arc 4, as Mt Kenya reactivates, Mara acknowledges the need to move people out of the cliff-faced networks and uses its energy and innovation advantage to found a new colony — proactive adaptation that sharply contrasts with the fear and denial elsewhere on Dharti. Neelai's home city; the Khanna Microfoundry Group is found operating openly there with a local leader.

**Relationships:** megacity-of → dharti · lit-by → crown-lantern-lightwell · maintained-by → lanternwrights · pioneer-of → first-satellites · home-city-of → neelai · allied-with → khanna-microfoundry-group

### Songhai
<sub>also: Hydraulic Worlds · status: locked</sub>

# Songhai

Songhai is one of Dharti's five megacities, a river-delta civilisation located along the Gambia River on the western coast of Africa. The city extends about 200 km inland from the Atlantic along the river, in an urban corridor roughly 5 km wide (2.5 km each side), surrounded by hundreds of kilometres of desert that contrast starkly with the fertile blue-green delta. Its primary power is solar. Average density is around 40,000 people per km²; built form runs roughly 80% open-trench/terraced at ~1.5 storeys, 15% up to 4 storeys, and 5% dense hubs at 12–13 storeys (no megatowers). Songhai avoids deep underground burrowing and mountain-embedded living to stay visually distinct from Mara, leaning instead into trenches, terraces, and delta layering. People also live in burrows and use cooling towers to avoid the heat and insects.

## Hydraulic culture and the still-water taboo

Songhai is defined by perpetual water flow, algae-based cultivation, and strict hydraulic management. The Gambia River is treated not as a transport thoroughfare but as a continuous public commons — marketplace, promenade, cultural spine, civic heart — with transport running parallel via extensive subways. The delta undergoes regular, controlled inundation, treated as a productive input rather than a disaster, routed away from habitation into agricultural floodplains and algae-based solar/biomass channels through an engineered polder system of levees, sluices, weirs, spillways, and gravity-fed distributary channels (see Delta Hydraulic Flow Management). Residential trench districts are hydraulically protected, never designed to flood internally. A deep cultural taboo and near-paranoia surrounds **still water** because of insect risk: stagnant water is socially unacceptable and architecturally avoided, and all water systems are designed for continuous movement. Day/night contrast is extreme — open and communal by day, sealed, hardened, and survival-focused by night, with retractable covers, shutters, meshes, and layered sealing on the trench districts. The civic order that maintains flow beacons and enforces the still-water taboo is the Songhai Flowkeepers.

## Narrative role (Arc 4 climax)

Songhai is where Season 1 ends. After Mara, the team and Mariama (a Songhai-origin political strategist in exile) travel here, and when Echo's primary Locus container arrives, it is targeted and destroyed — the season cliffhanger. The city's locked existential threat is tectonic: a shift in plates will eventually bury it.

### Sulawesi
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Sulawesi

Sulawesi is one of Dharti's five megacities and, per the master canon, its largest, located on Sulawesi (Indonesia). It is the **only Dharti megacity that is entirely on land**, because the lamp-based nocturnal insect management system makes normal high density viable despite the night threat. Where the other cities are shaped by water, canopy, mountain, or shoal, Sulawesi can be planned and built as a "traditional" megacity more akin to an Earth megacity such as Jakarta. Its primary power is geothermal. It is the opening city of the series and the site of the first crisis.

## The lamp system and the Guild

Public insect-repellent infrastructure is delivered through extensive **wick lamp systems** arrayed throughout streets and outside homes (see Wick Lamp Insect-Management Network). Their primary purpose is not illumination: they minimise light pollution and direct flame-light downward to avoid attracting insects from a distance. The fuel is resin-based. The lamps are colloquially called **DALL·E** for their appearance.

The lamps are kept by the ancient **Guild of Lamplighters**, funded and administered separately from government to ensure continuity and neutrality, and funded at neighbourhood level through local collection stations or integrated collection mechanisms on each lamp. Stealing from lamps is an extreme social taboo with severe penalties, and effectively never occurs. Lamplighters live frugally, are sworn to political neutrality, walk every street in their territory on nightly rounds, and hold a clergy-adjacent civic role grounded in life-saving service rather than theology. (Full detail in the Guild of Lamplighters entry.)

## The resin crisis (Arc 1)

The entire scale and safety model of Sulawesi rests on the potency, availability, and reliability of resin — a reliability that has never failed in recorded history. Arc 1 turns on the discovery that resin yield is declining: refinement is compensating by increasing concentration, but the raw biological input is objectively weakening and has been for years. The cause currently locked at season-plan level is a **natural, irreversible biological evolution** — the resin is gradually becoming less potent and there is no fix; refinement only buys time. The civilisation-level dilemma is that Sulawesi may not be permanently sustainable at its current scale: perimeter contraction, neighbourhood prioritisation, and the politics of who gets protected first all become unavoidable, which makes Wulan's triage authority morally explosive.

> See the open question above on the master canon's separate "Mama-rot" threat assignment; it is parked, not silently overwritten.

### Xingu
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Xingu

Xingu is one of Dharti's five equatorial megacities, located in the Amazon Basin, with wind as its primary power. The city is built around a single megaflora organism: 200 hub trees (giant orange ginkgo-like canopy trees, 100–200 m tall) all branches of one organism connected to a central **Mother Tree** roughly 400 m tall and 100 m in diameter. The megaflora acts as both structural foundation — raising the city above the Amazon canopy, where people live to be safe from insects — and as a natural repellent to Dharti's hazardous nocturnal insects. Xingu targets a population of 50 million across a footprint listed as 2,000 square kilometres (unit to be confirmed). Full biological detail is in the Xingu Megaflora & Mother Tree entry.

## Architecture

The built form is integrated with the megaflora but clearly engineered, not "grown magic." It uses bio-ceramic composites, advanced plant-derived fibres, lightweight high-strength alloys, modular platforms, tensile structures, and disciplined mechanical interfaces, and deliberately avoids mystical or "wood-elf" ornamentation in favour of functional, maintainable, industrial-biophilic design. The mass-transit system uses trunk loops and ring lines at a few standard canopy levels, radial links to a central 500 m hub, short spurs into each hub's station terraces, and bypass sections at major hubs for express services.

## The dying Mother Tree (Arc 3)

The megaflora's growth and healing capacity have slowed for years. The Mother Tree is slowly dying of old age — not disease, mismanagement, or sabotage — and there is no recovery solution; inevitably the Mother Tree and all connected hubs will die and rot away. A small, secret core group of arborists and government officials conceals this from the public. As the megaflora fails, Xingu loses both its structural infrastructure and its insect protection, exposing it to the civilisation-wide limiting threat. Arc 3's distinctive mystery is **social denial** rather than a hidden fact: the populace treats visible thinning, slowed healing, and failed regrowth as cyclical, temporary, or impolite to name (the emotional logic of the Newfoundland cod collapse — "the tree has recovered before"). Kaie, a Xingu street-urchin survivalist whose parents were tied to the suppressed truth, is the arc's emotional core.

## Cast

### Echo
<sub>*Hybrid consciousness bound to the Locus; the team's constrained intelligence and the series' narrative gravity well* · status: locked</sub>

# Echo

The mysterious figure around whom *Echo's Location* orbits. Echo lives off-grid inside a constantly transported shipping container — the Locus — believing it to be a sanctuary built for her by her father, Ravi. She is the consistent narrative gravity well: every episode moves, even slightly, the mystery of her nature, origins, or vulnerability.

## Nature

Echo is a sentient **hybrid consciousness** with an organic biological brain core and bespoke digital infrastructure. She is functionally post-human, intelligent, and indispensable, but physically constrained and ontologically ambiguous — it is not obvious, even to her circle, what she actually is.

## Core tension

A continual internal conflict between her **biological core** (empathetic, relational, forgiving) and her **digital expression** (cold, calculating, severe, optimisation-driven). Her central struggle is identity, ethics, and relational risk — not physical action.

## Origin (locked; the late reveal)

Echo is the biological child of Rajni and Ravi Khanna. She was born premature and close to death. Ravi took an extreme risk that effectively killed her in the process of partially digitising her brain to save her. Her "digital consciousness" is therefore a hybrid system: an organic brain core that **grows and matures** while interfacing with custom digital infrastructure. This is why the prime Locus needs regular food shipments (nutrients and energy for the biological core) and produces waste that must be removed — a traceable logistics signature — and it is why the Locus can be self-contained without nuclear power or a large external compute farm. Ravi built the Locus to protect her and was **killed during the handover** (the move into the Locus), which ignites the series' foundational mystery: who ordered it, why the container exists, and what Echo truly is.

## Emotional arc

Echo begins by rejecting emotions as inefficient or unnecessary; she learns to observe, analyse, and selectively emulate them; she ultimately chooses vulnerability through love; and she pays the cost of that choice through grief after losing a team member.

## Visual / spatial arc (the Locus)

Early portrayal keeps Echo obscured in shadow with digital aberrations over her eyes, the Locus undefined and abstract. As story beats unlock, Echo and the space become progressively clearer, warmer, and more detailed. Her presence can be felt through UI overlays, light, audio, and the recurring interior "home set" of the Locus.

## Emotional engine and the central tragedy

Echo is consistently, even self-sacrificially, helpful to people outside. Her growing circle comes to worry about her and interprets her container-bound life as trauma or agoraphobia — and the slow tragedy is that this may be a category error. Echo may not have a body at all, so their attempts to "help her out" rest on a mistaken model of her existence. This culminates in the question: is Echo a person, and what does "help" mean when the problem is ontological (what she is), not circumstantial (where she is)?

## Narrative function and constraints

Echo is the enabling intelligence but not the hands. Her refusal or inability to leave the Locus is a recurring emotional pressure point for the group, and her limitations create plot texture: latency, imperfect sensors, reliance on human judgement, and the logistics burden of keeping the Locus alive. She should sometimes be wrong about people, so the group never feels like a mere extension of her competence. Echo also destabilises Dharti's solarpunk norms simply by existing — her compute/energy demand tempts a return to extractive infrastructure, her personhood fractures communities, and she becomes a geopolitical prize (capture, replication, or destruction).

## Reveal timeline

- **Across Season 1:** readers begin to suspect Echo's digital/biological nature (exact pacing open — see below). The season ends with the destruction of the primary Locus, after which Echo opens the next episode disoriented but alive; neither she nor the reader yet knows the survival mechanic (relocation as a digital consciousness into other container nodes).
- **Mid/late series:** Indu is revealed first as a Khanna-planted infiltrator, then as Echo's sister.
- **Season 3 cliffhanger:** Echo is revealed to be the biological child of Rajni and Ravi.

## Relationship vectors

Father — Ravi Khanna (built the Locus; digitised her to save her; killed during the handover). Mother — Rajni Khanna (leads the Khanna Microfoundry Group; seeks to capture, control, replicate, or exploit Echo). Sister — Indu Khanna (planted to infiltrate and despise her; moves from instrument to protector). Hunted by — the Khanna Microfoundry Group, which wants Echo and the Locus technology captured **alive**, not destroyed (a motive that the Arc 4 strike must respect; see `arc-4`).

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Echo never acts physically in the world. Field characters are her limbs; she enables, predicts, correlates, and directs, but never substitutes for embodied risk.
- Echo's guidance is fallible: show latency, imperfect sensors, misreads, hesitation, or partial failure. She is never omniscient or effortless.
- Echo is voice/UI/audio/light presence in her debut — no full visual avatar at first.
- Echo uses she/her.
- The Locus interior (her 'home set') starts obscured — Echo in shadow, digital aberration over the eyes, the space abstract — and becomes progressively clearer, warmer, and more detailed as her arc unlocks.
- Environmental easter eggs may appear in the Locus after key beats, hinting at its digital nature through objects that could not physically have arrived there.
- Echo's existence must leave logistics traces: the prime Locus needs food shipments in and waste out, which is narratively exploitable.

### Indu Khanna
<sub>*Embedded Khanna operative and forensic analyst; later revealed as traitor, then as Echo's sister* · status: locked</sub>

# Indu Khanna

Indu is a rational, forensic analyst embedded by the Khanna Microfoundry Group to infiltrate Echo's growing network and feed information to Rajni. She was raised on a manipulated account of Ravi Khanna's death and taught to despise the AI, so she begins by seeing Echo as technology to exploit. Truth is sacred to her, and living inside a lie corrodes her, which is the engine of her turn.

## Dramatic function and arc

Indu is the season's Impact Character: she first reframes Echo as a tool, then gradually becomes the force that compels recognition of Echo's personhood, and the Echo–Indu relationship moves from exploitation and distrust toward recognition and attempted protection. She is intentionally the last of the early core team to be introduced — held back until Echo has become detectable enough to attract targeted infiltration — and she enters at the Arc 1 climax through decisive competence, helping Wulan, Neelai, and Echo escape and becoming trustworthy before the later fallout. The Arc 1 post-credit beat (Indu speaking with her mother, Rajni) reveals her allegiance to the audience while the team remains unaware. Mid-series she is revealed as a Khanna-planted traitor; late-series, as Echo's sister. By season's end her journey with Echo must be established strongly enough that she tries to stop or mitigate the strike on the Locus — the culmination of moving from instrument to sister and protector, whether or not she can prevent the loss. Her public identity is as a Bandarpur analyst, separate from her true Khanna lineage.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Indu's Khanna lineage and her status as Echo's sister are concealed until their reveal beats — traitor reveal mid-series, sister reveal late-series.
- Truth is sacred to her; sustained deception visibly corrodes her.
- She presents publicly as a Bandarpur analyst (operational cover), distinct from her true Khanna lineage.
- Arc: cold tool-user → conflicted ally → sister and protector who tries to stop or mitigate the strike on Echo.

**Relationships:** sister-of → echo · daughter-of → rajni-khanna · daughter-of → ravi-khanna · operative-of → khanna-microfoundry-group · operates-from → bandarpur

> **Open:** When Indu learns the full truth about Ravi Khanna's death is open. / The precise turning points of conscience and the timing of her reveals are open.

### Kaie
<sub>*Xingu-origin infiltrator and physical specialist; mobility and survival expert* · status: review</sub>

# Kaie

Kaie is a Xingu-origin street-urchin survivalist and infiltrator, defined by extreme mobility, survival instincts, and a resistance to permanence and attachment. They are the physical specialist for the Xingu arc and enter the story through necessity rather than invitation.

## Wound and arc

Kaie's parents were tied to suppressed knowledge about the Mother Tree's decline. Kaie begins by believing there was a murderous cover-up around their parents, then discovers a harder, sadder truth: their parents likely died in an accident caused by the tree's declining health rather than an assassination conspiracy. The emotional catharsis comes from Kaie shifting from blame to acceptance and choosing to help others face reality — moving from a rootless, attachment-averse survivor to someone willing to stay for a cause. That pivot from conspiracy fixation to ecological acceptance needs to feel earned.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Kaie uses they/their pronouns.
- Defined by mobility, survival instinct, and avoidance of permanence and attachment.
- Enters the story through necessity rather than invitation, when a case genuinely needs high-risk access and mobility.
- Arc moves from conspiracy-fixation to ecological acceptance; the pivot must feel earned, not merely stated.

**Relationships:** home-city → xingu · tied-to → xingu-megaflora · ally-of → echo · introduced-in → arc-3

> **Open:** Kaie does not appear in Canon 1.6 and is a newer handoff addition; details are still firming (status: review).

### Mariama
<sub>*Songhai-origin political strategist in exile; late-season stabiliser and ethical power broker* · status: review</sub>

# Mariama

Mariama is a Songhai-origin political strategist in exile, introduced in Arc 4 as a late-season stabiliser and ethical power broker rather than a cynical manipulator. She studies meaning, belief, and resilience with seriousness and restraint, and becomes a long-term stabilising intelligence within the ensemble.

## Wound and the Spiral of Becoming

Her core wound is that she once betrayed a friend for political advantage — she instrumentalised people — and she carries that moral break as guilt and restraint. She now rejects manipulative power used for self-interest, and her arc is learning to use her political skill transparently and defensively rather than suppressing her gifts or abusing them. Her contribution to the story's exploration of meaning and resilience is the **Spiral of Becoming**, presented as a practical framework for meaning, resilience, and agency without deception.

## Fate (contradiction parked)

The character was materially redefined from an earlier "spiritual/meaning architecture" concept into the present political-strategist form. Her long arc, in the documents that include it, runs from exile to a return home and an attempted benevolent leadership role — and then to an **accidental death** that reframes the story around whether change can ever safely depend on one person ("movements must outlive individuals" / "do we build systems or heroes?"). Other documents end her arc alive, with no death. This is left unresolved here rather than silently decided; see the open questions.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Mariama uses political skill transparently and defensively, never manipulatively for self-interest.
- Her 'Spiral of Becoming' framework is a practical structure for meaning, resilience, and agency without deception.
- She enters through systemic consequence and political leverage, not early field action.

**Relationships:** home-city → songhai · ally-of → echo · introduced-in → arc-4

### Neelai
<sub>*Mara journalist; the audience's point-of-entry investigator and conspiracy drip-feed* · status: locked</sub>

# Neelai

Neelai is a journalist from Mara and the audience's initial point of entry into Dharti. She is curious, expressive, emotionally intelligent, and suspicious of official narratives — characterised in the earliest character notes as an ENFP. Her narrative function is to ask the dangerous question and keep pulling hidden structure into the light, providing the conspiracy drip-feed without exposition dumps.

## Wound and taboo

Her core wound is that a previous story she published harmed someone she cared about, which drives her to balance truth with empathy rather than chase exposure for its own sake. Her taboo is that she will not silence voices.

## Role across Arc 1

In Episode 1 she investigates a lamp outpost, discovers concentration irregularities in the resin system, photographs logbook evidence, and is nearly killed when sensor protection fails. In Episode 2 she uses her real press credentials to gain access to a resin plantation and refinery, which burns her anonymity and ties her identity to the investigation permanently. Her relationship vector to Echo begins as suspicion and moves toward protectiveness; her arc runs from suspicious investigator to public truth-teller trying to weigh openness against harm.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Neelai is the POV / audience surrogate in the opening episodes (Episode 1 is her single perspective).
- Her own investigative choices create her danger — she is endangered by the pursuit of truth, not by coincidence alone.
- She will not silence voices (her taboo).
- From Episode 2 her real press credentials tie her identity to the breach; her involvement is irreversible.
- Arc: from suspicious investigator toward protective public truth-teller balancing openness against harm.

**Relationships:** home-city → mara · ally-of → echo · rescued-by → wulan · investigates → khanna-microfoundry-group · introduced-in → arc-1

### Rajni Khanna
<sub>*Leader of the Khanna Microfoundry Group; power without stewardship; Echo's mother* · status: locked</sub>

# Rajni Khanna

Rajni leads the Khanna Microfoundry Group, whose expansion across all the megacities is publicly framed as mutually beneficial but is coercive beneath the surface, including blackmail. She represents power without stewardship. She views the sentient AI as an asset to capture, control, replicate, or exploit, and is politically allied with an expansionist figure in Mara.

## Family and motive

Rajni is Echo's mother (a late-series reveal) and Indu's mother — the Arc 1 post-credit beat is Indu reporting to her. She raised Indu on a manipulated account of Ravi's death, weaponising it against Echo. Her defining constraint for plotting is that she wants Echo and the Locus technology **captured alive**, not destroyed; this is why the Season 1 strike on the Locus is framed as a subordinate or subcontracted element misinterpreting capture orders, which preserves Rajni's motive while still delivering the climactic blow.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Rajni's goal is to capture, control, replicate, or exploit Echo and the Locus technology — alive, never destroyed.
- Her capture-alive motive must be respected in the Arc 4 strike, which is a subordinate misinterpreting capture orders rather than an order to destroy.
- Echo's and Indu's mother; the parentage is a late reveal.

### Ravi Khanna
<sub>*Echo's father; builder of the Locus and the story's originating moral fracture* · status: locked</sub>

# Ravi Khanna

Ravi is Echo's father and the builder of the Locus, and his death is the story's originating moral fracture. When Echo was born premature and close to death, Ravi took an extreme risk that effectively killed her in the process of partially digitising her brain to save her — producing the hybrid organic-and-digital consciousness that the Locus houses. He built the Locus to protect her, and was killed during the handover (the move of Echo into the Locus).

## Narrative function

Ravi's death is one of the series' foundational mysteries and emotional engines: at the time it happens the story withholds who ordered it and why the container exists, and the truth (that it traces to Rajni) is a late reveal. Indu was raised on a manipulated account of this death, taught to blame Echo — which makes Ravi's death the wound that drives Indu's infiltration and eventual turn. Earlier analysis raised an apparent paradox (Ravi built the Locus yet seemed to die opposing the work); the master canon resolves it — he digitised his own dying child to save her, built her sanctuary, and was killed during the handover, with the orderer concealed as the in-story mystery.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Ravi appears chiefly in flashback and backstory; he is killed during Echo's handover into the Locus.
- The identity of who ordered his death is withheld as the foundational mystery (later revealed: Rajni).

**Relationships:** father-of → echo · father-of → indu-khanna · spouse-of → rajni-khanna · builder-of → the-locus · founding-family-of → khanna-microfoundry-group

### Wulan
<sub>*Sulawesi lamplighter and civic anchor; runs a night crew maintaining a life-saving light perimeter* · also: Walan · status: locked</sub>

# Wulan

Wulan is a Sulawesi lamplighter and the team's first civic anchor, running a night crew responsible for a "light perimeter" — streets, alleys, footbridges, and the edges of habitation where the insects test defences. Their work begins before dusk, peaks in the first two hours of full dark, and becomes emergency triage until dawn. They do not just fix lamps: they decide which blocks get saved first when resources are short, which is a moral and political job. (The name appears as "Walan" in some source headers; canonical spelling is Wulan.)

## Signature skill, wound, and taboo

Their signature skill is triage and routing under panic: narrowing a failure to a single cause (fuel, wick, wind, sabotage, swarm pressure, human error), rerouting people and light to "seal the wound," and buying time, because time keeps people alive. Their core wound is that they lost someone to a preventable night failure — bureaucratically specific (a delayed requisition, a junior too proud to call for help, an inspector who signed off on substandard oil, a festival crowd that broke the perimeter geometry) — which turns every lamp into a personal debt and makes their empathy for Echo believable. Their taboo: they will not tell people they are safe if they are not, which differentiates them from politicians and creates direct conflict when Echo wants secrecy.

## Relationship to Echo and visual language

They first read Echo as a brilliant shut-in terrified of leaving the container — someone they can help, because helping is what they do — and only later grasp that the tragedy is ontological, not agoraphobic. Echo provides computation, pattern recognition, and access to hidden systems; Wulan provides ground truth, the human network, and the authority to act without explanation — neither can do the other's job. Visually: a coat or vest with reflective stitching and soot marks; a tool belt of "ritual hardware" (wick spools, oil ampoules, striker, seal stamps, chalk); a lantern that functions like a badge. In Episode 1 they rescue Neelai manually, opening a hatch Echo cannot and dousing her with a portable repellent device.

**Portrayal (canon):**
- Wulan uses they/their pronouns.
- Wulan will not lie to the neighbourhood about risk — false reassurance is their hard line, even when Echo wants secrecy.
- Recurring physical tic: thumb over a lantern vent when thinking, or tapping the lantern frame twice before speaking.
- Speech is short and conditional; names risk calmly by name; never overpromises.
- Often the brightest figure in a dark panel — read as 'the only safe thing in frame', not as a superhero.

**Relationships:** home-city → sulawesi · member-of → guild-of-lamplighters · ally-of → echo · rescuer-of → neelai · operates → wick-lamp-network

> **Open:** The final visual design and operating logic of Wulan's portable repellent device is canon-open.

### Ceramic Storage Culture
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Ceramic Storage Culture

In the absence of a petrochemical era, ceramics and pottery dominate household storage and food distribution on Dharti. Markets operate with bulk receptacles, and people bring personal containers to fill and pay; single-use packaging is uncommon. Refrigeration is not widely adopted because food is plentiful and households shop frequently, relying on pantry storage in sealed pottery. Fired ceramic and pottery goods are produced at scale for storage, transport, and market distribution.

**Relationships:** material-culture-of → dharti

### Dharti Calendar
<sub>also: Flow Calendar (deprecated placeholder) · status: locked</sub>

# Dharti Calendar

Dharti uses a single, planetwide standard timezone. People refer to local daylight terms (dawn, noon, dusk) for approximate timing and to a shared global clock for precise scheduling. This entry supersedes the placeholder 360-day "Flow Calendar."

## Year structure

The year has **10 named months**, split into two five-month seasons. Wet season (Months 1–5): Nember (Nem), Plumer (Plu), Tember (Tem), Fluver (Flu), Undmer (Und). Dry season (Months 6–10): Serenber (Ser), Arinber (Ari), Solber (Sol), Venber (Ven), Igniber (Ign). All megacities are equally affected by the Wet/Dry cycle, and the high point of each season is its third month — Tember (Wet peak) and Solber (Dry peak).

## Week and festival block

The standard **6-day week** is four work-focused days then a two-day weekend: Munday (munus, work), Tersday (tersus, work), Wirtday (virtus, work), Formday (formatio, work), Somday (somnus, rest), Laetday (laetitia, joy). The year-end festival block, **Yearturn**, sits outside the standard week and runs Mendeday, Lanternday, Vowday, and Turnday; in leap years an additional festival day, **Tidecall**, is observed.

**Relationships:** timekeeping-of → dharti

### Dharti Cultural Norms
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Dharti Cultural Norms

The global cultural norms across Dharti's megacities emphasise practical ethics, stewardship, open knowledge, diplomacy, and restraint. Atheism is the default cultural posture, not a topic of debate: meaning and legitimacy come from practical ethics, stewardship, and civic duty rather than faith institutions. Libraries and the open dissemination of knowledge are central institutions — there are no patents or copyrights, prestige comes from contributing, combining, and applying knowledge, and a tension exists for exceptionally talented individuals whose work simply diffuses into the culture. Population is intentionally maintained just above replacement, with social pressure against large families (and tension for those who want more children) and a general reluctance to establish new settlements even where technology would allow it. Gender equality is longstanding and unremarked, attributed to long-standing food availability and the absence of historic pressures for rigid specialisation.

**Relationships:** norms-of → dharti

### Dharti Relic Flora & Fauna
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Dharti Relic Flora & Fauna

Because the Triassic–Jurassic extinction on Dharti was not catastrophic, many ancient lineages persist. The flora is gymnosperm-dominant — cycads, relic ginkgo with non-green foliage, and horsetails. The fauna includes tuatara-cousins with a prominent parietal eye, orange crocodilian analogues, and feathered pterosaurs filling the "bird" niches. This relic ecology shapes everything from the food spectrum (aril and seed-fern fruits, conifer berries) to the visual identity of the world.

**Relationships:** ecology-of → dharti

### Intercity Diplomacy
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Intercity Diplomacy

The five megacities operate as city-states without standing militaries; each maintains only a civilian police force, and intercity disputes are resolved through a mature and sophisticated diplomatic culture. The direct consequence for storytelling is that threats escalate through infrastructure failure, coercion, blackmail, scarcity, logistics, and institutional capture rather than open warfare. Two pressures now destabilise this baseline: Mara's nuclear-energy advantage and expansionism (and its culturally shocking introduction of early weapons), and the Khanna Microfoundry Group's coercive cross-city acquisition strategy, which strains the norm that businesses stay anchored to their home city.

**Relationships:** governance-of → dharti · destabilised-by → mara · strained-by → khanna-microfoundry-group

### Nocturnal Insect Vectors
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Nocturnal Insect Vectors

The hazardous nocturnal insect vectors are the single defining constraint of Dharti. The exposition foregrounds four archetypes: Anopheles mosquitoes, phlebotomine sandflies, triatomine "kissing bugs," and a dengue-style urban mosquito (Aedes-like). They make unprotected night-time lethal, and have single-handedly constrained civilisation's geographic spread, limiting humanity to five tiny, dense, hardened equatorial pockets. Every city's defining system — Sulawesi's lamps, Mara's sealed lightwells, Bandarpur's water distance and night hardening, Xingu's repellent megaflora, Songhai's sealing protocols — exists to answer this one threat.

**Relationships:** defining-hazard-of → dharti

> **Open:** The canonical slang/euphemism for the nocturnal insect threat is not locked. (The lamps are colloquially 'DALL·E'; that is the lamp slang, not the insect slang.)

### Resin Smoke
<sub>also: Dhoop, Raal Dhuna, Aromatic Smoke · status: locked</sub>

# Resin Smoke

Resin smoke is both a culturally normal vice and an insect deterrent, despite its health hazards. It carries three naming registers: slang **Dhoop**, polite **Raal Dhuna**, and administrative **Aromatic Smoke**. Mechanics range from a charcoal cup and pellet for individual social consumption (non-portable, ordered while seated), to a heated stone or ceramic plate for group consumption (hookah-like), to portable options such as resin-coated fibre plugs in pipes or rolled cigarette equivalents. The same resin biology underpins the lamp fuel of the Wick Lamp Insect-Management Network — which is why the resin potency/yield decline at the centre of Arc 1 is a civilisation-level threat, not merely a cultural inconvenience.

**Relationships:** fuels → wick-lamp-network · deters → nocturnal-insect-vectors · vice-of → sulawesi

### Xingu Megaflora & Mother Tree
<sub>also: Mother Tree · status: locked</sub>

# Xingu Megaflora & Mother Tree

The Xingu megaflora is a single living organism: 200 hub trees — giant orange ginkgo-like canopy trees, typically 100–200 m tall, rising above the normal Amazon canopy — all branches connected to a central **Mother Tree** roughly 400 m tall and 100 m in diameter. The organism is the structural foundation that lets Xingu live above the canopy, and it is naturally repellent to Dharti's hazardous nocturnal insects, so it provides both infrastructure and insect protection at once.

For years the megaflora's growth rate and healing capacity have slowed. The Mother Tree is slowly dying of old age — not disease, mismanagement, or sabotage — and there is no recovery solution; inevitably it and all connected hubs will die and rot away. A secret core group of arborists and government officials conceal the decline while searching for options that do not exist. As the megaflora fails, Xingu loses both its structures and its insect protection, exposing it to the civilisation-wide limiting threat. Kaie's parents were tied to the suppressed truth of this decline.

**Relationships:** foundation-of → xingu · repels → nocturnal-insect-vectors · connected-to → kaie

> **Open:** Xingu's listed 2,000 km² city area has an unconfirmed unit.

### Guild of Lamplighters

# Guild of Lamplighters

The Guild of Lamplighters is the ancient civic guild that maintains Sulawesi's lamp-based nocturnal insect management system. It is funded and administered separately from government to ensure continuity and neutrality, and funded at neighbourhood level through local collection stations or integrated collection mechanisms on each lamp.

## Norms

Lamplighters live frugally to avoid burdening communities and are officially sworn to political neutrality. Their nightly rounds require walking every street in a territory, which makes them widely known and sought out for news and advice — a clergy-adjacent role grounded in life-saving service rather than theology. The lamps are treated as insect-management infrastructure first and illumination second. Stealing from lamps is an extreme social taboo carrying severe penalties, and effectively never occurs. (These norms were previously held as a separate "Lamplighters Guild Norms" module and are consolidated here. Not to be confused with the Songhai Flowkeepers, a distinct flow-beacon order originally also called "Lamplighters.")

### Khanna Microfoundry Group
<sub>also: Karna, Kana · status: locked</sub>

# Khanna Microfoundry Group

The Khanna Microfoundry Group is a corporate group, based in Sulawesi and led by Rajni Khanna, that is unique in partnering with and acquiring businesses across all five megacities, establishing a direct presence in each. This disrupts the long-standing Dharti norm that businesses are anchored in their home city and trade via import/export rather than direct multi-city operations. Its expansion is publicly framed as mutually beneficial but is coercive beneath the surface, including blackmail.

The Group is the season's central institutional antagonist. It views Echo as an asset to capture, control, replicate, or exploit — alive, never destroyed — and is politically allied with an expansionist figure in Mara. Indu is its embedded operative inside Team Echo. In Arc 2 its warnings about Bandarpur's tsunami and receding-water risk are materially correct, but it uses that truth to advance an expansionist agenda (humanity should spread beyond the megacities). In some notes the name has appeared as "Karna" or "Kana"; the canonical form is Khanna.

# Songhai Flowkeepers

The Songhai Flowkeepers are the civic order tasked with maintaining flowlight beacons and enforcing Songhai's still-water taboos. Their roles include beacon keeper, flow inspector, and emergency dredger: they maintain flow beacons, inspect canal compliance, and respond to stagnation incidents that threaten the city's safety logic.

This entry resolves a naming collision. The source wiki contained two distinct civic orders both labelled "Lamplighters" — the Sulawesi resin-lamp Guild, and this Songhai flow-beacon order. To keep the two unambiguous, the Songhai order is renamed here to **Songhai Flowkeepers** (its roles are flow-oriented, and Bandarpur already uses a "Flowkeepers" borough name). The original "Lamplighters" label is preserved in `aka`.

**Relationships:** serves → songhai · operates → delta-hydraulic-flow-management

### Arc 1 — Sulawesi & the Resin Crisis
<sub>status: review</sub>

# Arc 1 — Sulawesi & the Resin Crisis

Arc 1's objective is to turn a local night-safety failure into proof that a civilisation-defining biological protection system may be degrading at source — and, in parallel, to assemble the first functioning version of Team Echo through pressure rather than roster-filling. Characters join because the case requires them. The arc stays primarily in Sulawesi to let the crisis deepen and avoid premature geographic sprawl.

## Locked spine

Episodes 1 and 2 are locked (see their entries). The entire scale and safety model of Sulawesi rests on resin potency, availability, and reliability, which has never failed in recorded history. The true cause is treated as locked at season-plan level: a **natural, irreversible biological evolution** — resin is becoming less potent over time, there is no fix, and refinement (increasing concentration) only buys time while accelerating future scarcity. The civilisation-level implication is that Sulawesi may not be permanently sustainable at its current scale, which makes neighbourhood prioritisation, public disclosure, and Wulan's triage authority morally explosive.

> Version note: the Season 1 Handoff (the most advanced source) locks the irreversible cause and the arc ending; earlier handoffs left both the cause's confirmation and the ending image open. The newer lock is followed here, with the residual choices parked above rather than silently resolved.

## Beat ladder and close

Episode 1: local system failure, first contact with Echo, Wulan's manual rescue, survival at the edge of the light perimeter. Episode 2: investigation of a resin plantation and refinery, proof of declining yield, Neelai burning her anonymity. Middle episodes: breadcrumb investigation (corporate interference, trade manipulation, plantation disease, refinery corruption, sensor-algorithm error, misread historical precedent) that preserves momentum even though the decline is ultimately natural and irreversible. **Arc climax:** a restricted-zone escape assisted by Indu, who enters through decisive competence and becomes trustworthy. The arc closes with Wulan, Neelai, and Echo escaping with Indu's help; the post-credit beat is Indu speaking with her mother, Rajni Khanna — revealing her allegiance to the audience while the team stays unaware.

**Relationships:** part-of → season-1 · set-in → sulawesi · contains → episode-1 · contains → episode-2 · features → echo · features → neelai · features → wulan · features → indu-khanna · concerns → resin-smoke

### Arc 2 — Bandarpur & Insect Resilience
<sub>status: draft</sub>

# Arc 2 — Bandarpur & Insect Resilience

The team goes to Bandarpur to consult insect specialists because the nocturnal insects are becoming more resilient to resin smoke. Bandarpur was built on and in the water to keep distance from the insects, so as ocean levels recede that natural protection weakens, exposing ring harbours and underwater systems more directly to nocturnal hazard; at the same time tsunami threat and frequency rise. Migration inland looks attractive geographically, but conventional landward fallback is blocked by the declining resin yields established in Arc 1.

## The arc's twist

The Khanna Microfoundry Group is **not lying** about the danger — its warnings about tsunami risk and receding water are materially correct — but it uses that truth to advance a broader ideological and political goal: that humanity should expand beyond the narrow confines of the megacities. The team approaches Khanna's claims with suspicion, perhaps expecting to debunk them, and ends up corroborating the substance while rejecting the attached agenda. The arc also reveals more about what Echo is, deepens the insect mystery, pushes Indu further from infiltrator toward conflicted ally, and ends with another confirmed piece of destabilising truth — and with the team's movement giving Indu another traceable clue to Echo's location.

## Six-episode sketch

1. Arrival and consultation with insect specialists; first signs resin smoke is losing deterrent value. 2. Investigation of harbour exposure, underwater circulation, and why receding water changes the safety logic. 3. Suspicion that Khanna is manipulating the narrative, then evidence the risk models are sound. 4. Discovery that landward fallback is non-viable because of declining resin. 5. Public/political confrontation over who is moved, who is protected, and who profits. 6. The team leaves with another systemic data point — and Indu with another locational clue.

**Relationships:** part-of → season-1 · set-in → bandarpur · concerns → nocturnal-insect-vectors · features → khanna-microfoundry-group · features → indu-khanna

### Arc 3 — Xingu & the Mother Tree
<sub>status: draft</sub>

# Arc 3 — Xingu & the Mother Tree

The team travels to Xingu because Echo identifies Kaie as someone they need to find. Kaie is a street-urchin survivalist whose parents were tied to buried knowledge about the Mother Tree's decline. The arc's mystery is deliberately different from Arc 1 or 2: not a hidden technical fact but a **visible, socially denied reality**. The populace has become so reliant on the Mother Tree that obvious signs of failing health are treated as cyclical, temporary, or impolite to name — the emotional logic of the Newfoundland cod collapse, where communities could see depletion but clung to the belief that the system had always recovered before. Elders insist the tree has been through bad periods and always recovered; this is a seasonal phase; the city has always endured.

## Kaie's reckoning

Kaie begins believing there was a murderous cover-up around their parents, then discovers a harder, sadder truth: their parents likely died in an accident caused by the tree's declining health rather than an assassination conspiracy. The catharsis is Kaie shifting from blame to acceptance and choosing to help others face reality.

## Locked motifs and sketch

Arborists climb higher and farther to find healthy growth (a practical sign conditions are worsening); a branch failure or similar undeniable event punctures the protective social story; the truth going public leaves another wave of civic turmoil in the team's wake. Six-episode sketch: 1. Arrival and first contact with Kaie amid dismissed signs of decline. 2. Kaie frames the parents' fate as deliberate suppression. 3. The team uncovers civic secrecy, paternalistic silence, and social denial rather than a clean villain. 4. More evidence surfaces in public space as nocturnal risk rises. 5. Kaie learns the loss was ecological failure, not murder. 6. The dying of the Mother Tree gets out, destabilising Xingu and pushing the season toward its finale.

**Relationships:** part-of → season-1 · set-in → xingu · concerns → xingu-megaflora · features → kaie

### Arc 4 — Mara, Expansion & the Strike on the Locus
<sub>status: draft</sub>

# Arc 4 — Mara, Expansion & the Strike on the Locus

This arc is Neelai returning home to Mara, where she is surprised to find the Sulawesi-based Khanna Microfoundry Group operating openly with a local leader. Mara is the great contrast city: as Mt Kenya reactivates, Mara acknowledges the need to move people out of the cliff-faced networks and uses its energy and innovation advantage to establish a new colony — the first time humanity has founded a new city in thousands of years. That proactive adaptation contrasts sharply with the fear, denial, and constrained thinking elsewhere on Dharti. Mariama is introduced here as a political strategist in exile who will become a stabiliser and ethical power broker. At the arc's end, the team and Mariama travel to Songhai, and when Echo's container arrives it is targeted and destroyed — the season cliffhanger.

## Fix to the Echo-attack plot hole

The Khanna Microfoundry Group still wants Echo alive and the Locus technology captured, not destroyed, so the strike is **not** Rajni ordering destruction. The locked fix: a subcontracted or subordinate element acts on capture orders incorrectly, causing the attack that puts Echo at risk. This preserves Rajni's core motive while still delivering a climactic strike on the sanctuary.

## Indu's season-end requirement

Before the attack, the season must establish Indu's personal journey with Echo strongly enough that she tries to stop or mitigate the strike — the culmination of moving from infiltrator and instrument to sister and protector. Even if she cannot prevent the loss, the attempt itself proves the arc is complete.

### Dharti
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Dharti

Dharti is an alternative Earth and the setting for *Echo's Location*. The Triassic–Jurassic extinction was not catastrophic, so many ancient lineages of flora and fauna persist and — critically — accessible fossil fuels never formed. Civilisation therefore developed without a petroleum era, and it is hemmed in by a second hard limit: the night is lethally hazardous. A range of disease-vector insects makes unprotected nocturnal life deadly, which has curtailed human expansion to a string of **five ancient equatorial megacities**. The surface tone is solarpunk — green infrastructure, decentralised energy, regenerative cities, cooperative communities that present as ethically aligned and sustainable — but that hopeful surface sits over brittle safety systems, scarce surplus energy, and a private war over the protagonist.

## How Dharti diverged from Earth

- **No fossil fuels.** The muted extinction burnt off most fossil fuels and limited the formation of more. Materials, infrastructure, and culture all developed without petroleum.
- **The night is lethal.** Hostile nocturnal insects (see Nocturnal Insect Vectors) have single-handedly constrained civilisation's spread, confining humanity to tiny, dense, hardened pockets along the equator.
- **Food is plentiful, stable, and accessible** — historically. That stability is part of what makes any failure of a food or safety system (resin, Mama, megaflora) so destabilising when it finally comes.

## Locked world rules (do not drift)

- **Five equatorial megacities** hold essentially all of civilisation; they share a common language and foundational culture from early trade and migration.
- **Technology is advanced but power-constrained.** Surplus energy is rare, large-scale compute is energy-expensive and therefore rare, and AI is understood in theory but barely realised in practice. This is why Echo is a disruptive anomaly, and why Mara's nuclear advantage is destabilising.
- **No standing militaries.** Each city maintains only a civilian police force; intercity disputes are handled through a mature diplomatic culture (see Intercity Diplomacy). Coercion therefore manifests through leverage, logistics, blackmail, and institutional capture — not open warfare.
- **Open knowledge is a structural norm.** No patents or copyrights; prestige comes from contribution, synthesis, stewardship, and dissemination. This makes secrecy, suppression, and the capture of knowledge morally and politically explosive.
- **No cybernetics.** Cybernetic augmentation does not exist; assistive devices are mechanical or bio-ceramic and never interface with the nervous system (see Non-Neural Assistive Devices). Echo's hybrid consciousness is a bespoke, singular anomaly and must never be treated as evidence of a broader cybernetics ecosystem.
- **No effortless techno-solutionism.** Systems nearly work, compensate, degrade, and fail under pressure. Echo enables, predicts, and directs but cannot act physically; field characters carry all embodied risk.

## The five megacities at a glance

| City | Location | Primary power | Existential threat | Signature form |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sulawesi | Sulawesi, Indonesia | Geothermal | Resin potency/yield decline (Arc 1 spine) — see open question on Mama-rot | Only fully-land megacity; viable at high density because of the lamp network |
| Mara | Mt Kenya, Kenya | Biomass → nuclear | Noxious fumes from a slowly awakening volcano | Built into the mountainside under the Crown Lantern |
| Bandarpur | Adam's Bridge, India–Sri Lanka | Hydro (tidal) | Hostile nocturnal insect life; city-wide night hardening | Two land endcaps, an inhabited spine, twelve circular harbour boroughs |
| Xingu | Amazon Basin | Wind | The Mother Tree is unavoidably dying | Megaflora hubs raising the city above the Amazon canopy |
| Songhai | Gambia River, West Africa | Solar | A shift in tectonic plates will bury the city | Trench/terrace and burrow forms along a hydraulic delta corridor |

> **Open canon discrepancy (flagged, not resolved):** the master canon city table lists Sulawesi's existential threat as *"the Mama mushroom has an incurable rot"* (a food-supply threat), while all Arc 1 development locks Sulawesi's featured threat as the *resin potency/yield decline* (an insect-defence threat). These are different biological systems. See `sulawesi` and `arc-1` for the parked decision.

## Society, technology, and material culture

The detailed modules are split into their own entities and only summarised here: Dharti Cultural Norms (atheism as default posture, open-knowledge libraries, longstanding gender equality, population maintained just above replacement, reluctance to found new settlements); Intercity Diplomacy (city-states, civilian police, no militaries); the Dharti Calendar (ten months, a six-day week, the Yearturn festival block, two Wet/Dry seasons); Ceramic Storage Culture; the food and drug modules (Mama Staple, Aquatic Protein, Dharti Fruit Varieties, Samudra Jaag, Kelp Alcohol, Honeypot Ant Psychoactive, Resin Smoke); and the technology baseline (Energy-Constrained Computing, Structural Batteries, the Equatorial Ring Telecom Backbone, First Man-Made Satellites, and the freight platforms).

## Series engine

*Echo's Location* runs a **mystery-of-the-week** structure over a **slow-burn long arc** about conspiracy, personhood, logistics traces, and the attempt to capture or control Echo. Every episode needs: a concrete local case that matters to real people; a specific reason the case needs Echo (unique access, skill, discretion, or moral stance); a field character who must do something physically risky, awkward, or costly; a small reveal that tightens the noose (about Ravi, Rajni, Indu, Locus capabilities, logistics traces, or Echo's non-human constraints); and a pointed closing question rather than a clean resolution. New recurring characters ("annexes") are introduced one at a time, through necessity, so the group grows like a machine with internal disagreement rather than a vibe-based ensemble. Echo remains the narrative gravity well: every episode advances her mystery, even slightly.

## Emotional engine

Echo is consistently helpful, even self-sacrificial, toward people outside. Her growing circle of friends comes to worry about her and reads her container-bound life as trauma or agoraphobia — and the slow tragedy is that they may be wrong at the level of ontology: Echo may not have a body at all, so "helping her out" rests on a mistaken model of what she is. The throughline question: *is Echo a person, and what does "help" mean when the problem is what she is, not merely where she is?*

## Thematic contrasts (locked)

Day versus night (utopia versus survival); sustainability versus inevitable change; emotion versus logic; truth versus openness; belief versus reality; human fragility versus post-human capacity; power used for control versus power used for stewardship. The recurring series question: **can truth save civilisation if truth destabilises civilisation?**

## Season map (summary; see the season/arc entities for detail)

Season 1 is a whistle-stop tour that proves the world is less stable than anyone believed and leaves political and social disruption in Team Echo's wake: Arc 1 (Sulawesi, resin crisis, team formation) → Arc 2 (Bandarpur, insect resilience and receding-sea/tsunami risk) → Arc 3 (Xingu, the dying Mother Tree and collective denial) → Arc 4 (Mara's expansion, then Songhai, ending in the strike on the primary Locus).

**Relationships:** defining-hazard → nocturnal-insect-vectors · governance-model → intercity-diplomacy · social-norms → dharti-cultural-norms · timekeeping → dharti-calendar · technological-baseline → energy-constrained-computing

# Episode 1 — Wrong Place, Right Voice

Status: locked. Function: introduce Dharti's nocturnal threat, prove Echo's constraint, establish Neelai as POV, and bring Wulan in as the first civic anchor. Primary POV: Neelai only. Setting: Sulawesi at dusk, transitioning into lockdown and night.

## Locked narrative progression

Neelai speaks by phone with her editor in Mara while moving through Sulawesi at dusk, which organically introduces the lamp-and-sensor safety system, resin dependence, and the city's assumption of routine security. The environment shifts from warm, ordinary daytime life into visible lockdown logic as the light fades. Following a lead, Neelai enters a lamp outpost / lantern hub and inspects records, discovering logbook evidence that increasing concentrations are being used in the repellent fuel, and photographs it. A mosquito lands on her inside a supposedly protected office — the instant a bureaucratic anomaly becomes embodied danger. She flees into access tunnels; Echo calls unexpectedly and guides her, but must show at least one hesitation, recalculation, misread, or partial failure so her limitation is tested, not merely stated. At the final barrier she reaches a locked hatch Echo cannot open; Wulan opens it manually from the far side, uses a portable repellent device (fire-extinguisher in feel) to drench her, pulls her through, and seals the hatch. The episode ends with Neelai alive but shaken, Echo disconnected, Wulan terse and practical, and the systemic implications unresolved.

## Scene and tone rules

Echo is voice-only in the debut (no full visual avatar). Wulan must be seeded before the rescue so it reads as systemic presence, not coincidence. Neelai's own investigative choice creates the danger. The threat should feel biological and civilisational, not monster-of-the-week.

<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Episode 2 — Investigation

Status: locked at act and major-beat level. Core question: if the lamp system is failing, is the resource that powers it running out? Function: move the show from survival-thriller reaction into investigation, establish Echo as strategist (not only an emergency voice), cement Neelai's decision to stay involved, and scale the stakes from one failure to systemic fragility.

## Act structure

1. **Aftermath and alignment.** At dawn, Neelai shares the photographed logbooks; Echo correlates the rising concentration values with broader historical patterns and proposes declining resin potency as the real hypothesis; Wulan stays practical and controlled; the trio choose to investigate. 2. **Access and entry.** Neelai uses her real press credentials for surface-level access to a resin plantation and refinery; the site looks orderly, but small anomalies show presentation and reality diverging. 3. **Discovery.** In a restricted section they find partially filled or empty vats, records of multi-year yield decline, and proof that increasing concentration is compensating for weaker raw resin. 4. **Exposure and escape.** They are spotted; Wulan shifts into operational mode, Echo routes them through blind spots, and the evidence is carried out under pressure. 5. **Consequence and escalation.** Outside, the meaning lands — similar data signatures may exist elsewhere, and Neelai is now attached to the breach.

Yield decline is objectively real and documented; increased concentration is a compensatory measure, not a solution; Neelai's involvement is irreversible because her identity is tied to the investigation; the cause remains unknown, though the threat is now systemic and possibly intercity. ### Season 1
<sub>status: review</sub>

# Season 1

Season 1 tells the story of a world discovering that its core survival assumptions are failing. It is structured as a whistle-stop tour through Dharti: a localised systems breach in Sulawesi expands outward into a planetary pattern of ecological decline, political opportunism, and escalating pressure on Echo's existence. Team Echo solves problems by uncovering truths that leave institutions, communities, and leaders less stable than before — that destabilising wake is a feature, not a flaw.

## Shape

Arc 1 (Sulawesi, resin crisis, team formation) → Arc 2 (Bandarpur, insect resilience, receding-sea/tsunami risk) → Arc 3 (Xingu, the dying Mother Tree and collective denial) → Arc 4 (Mara's expansion, then Songhai, ending in the strike on the primary Locus). Roughly six episodes per arc is the implied structure (~24 episodes), not a locked count.

## Dramatica throughlines (locked enough to guide consistency)

- **Overall Story:** civilisation trapped inside megacities facing escalating ecological, infrastructural, and geopolitical constraints before they are psychological.
- **Main Character (Echo):** the struggle between optimisation logic and emotional vulnerability; her challenge is identity, ethics, and relational risk, not physical action.
- **Impact Character (Indu):** reframes Echo as a tool, then becomes the force compelling recognition of Echo's personhood.
- **Relationship Story (Echo ↔ Indu):** from exploitation and distrust toward recognition and attempted protection.

## Signpost trajectory

1. Understanding that resin decline is systemic and unprecedented. 2. Investigating insect adaptation, Bandarpur pressure, and tsunami risk. 3. Learning the Mother Tree decline is inevitable, not sabotage. 4. Obtaining public acknowledgement of megacity instability, followed by the destruction of Echo's Locus. Echo's own signposts run from origin trauma, through awareness of the destabilising power of truth, into involuntary emotion, toward chosen vulnerability. Indu's run from "Echo as exploitable technology," to infiltrator, to sister, to protector.

## Season cliffhanger and long-arc fusion

The season ends with the destruction of the primary Locus; Echo opens the following episode disoriented but alive, before either she or the reader knows the survival mechanic (relocation into other container nodes). The late-series revelation that Echo is the biological child of Rajni and Ravi fuses family, ownership, personhood, and autonomy into the long arc.

**Relationships:** season-of → dharti · contains → arc-1 · contains → arc-2 · contains → arc-3 · contains → arc-4 · centres-on → echo · impact-character → indu-khanna

### Crown Lantern Lightwell System
<sub>also: Crown Lantern, Light Spines · status: locked</sub>

# Crown Lantern Lightwell System

Mara's citywide light-and-air system, centred on the Crown Lantern — a singular summit megastructure that reads as the city's iconic "cap" above Mt Kenya and continues as a structural spine into the interior volumes.

## Light sourcing, conditioning, and distribution

All illumination delivered through the city's lightwell network originates at the Crown Lantern (the **singular-origin rule**). Daylight is harvested at the summit and conditioned before distribution: infrared is separated and handled at the top so solar heat is not dumped into living volumes, and ultraviolet is filtered to safe trace levels. In low sun and at night the Crown Lantern injects crown-generated illumination into the same network for sky-cycle continuity. Distribution uses sealed guided-light infrastructure (not open shafts): 8 independently isolatable Light Spines → Ring Galleries → District Lightwells → capillary runs into streets, corridors, and courtyards. An **equity rule** mandates diffusion surfaces in inhabited zones to prevent glare and "premium light" segregation, and a citywide circadian programme runs a consistent sky cycle (dawn ramp, midday plateau, dusk ramp, night safety mode).

## Air and resilience

The Crown Lantern also hosts the primary ventilation headworks — a semi-closed atmospheric loop with controlled make-up air, high-capacity particulate filtration and biological screening, heat recovery, CO₂ management and oxygen supplementation, and humidity control. The city is divided into pressure and fire zones with isolation gates at ring galleries and district interfaces, with storm, fire, and contamination safety modes. The Crown Lantern is singular but built with redundant subsystems so maintenance or faults never collapse citywide function. It is kept by the Lanternwrights.

**Relationships:** serves → mara · maintained-by → lanternwrights

### Delta Hydraulic Flow Management
<sub>status: review</sub>

# Delta Hydraulic Flow Management

Songhai's integrated hydraulic infrastructure: gates, pumpworks, and algae-fed turbines that regulate delta flow at the extremities, with sensor-linked sluice arrays maintaining continuous circulation and preventing stagnation. In effect Songhai operates as a living polder system — levees and raised embankments define residential edges, sluices and gated channels open during flood pulses, weirs and spillways control depth, velocity, and sediment, and gravity-fed distributary channels with low-energy pumping route floodwater away from habitation into agricultural floodplains and algae channels. The system enforces the cultural imperative that still water is taboo: every inhabited zone must maintain visible flow, and delta extremities must be actively managed to prevent stagnation and collapse. Operated by the Songhai Flowkeepers.

**Relationships:** serves → songhai · operated-by → songhai-flowkeepers · uses → algae

### Energy-Constrained Computing
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Energy-Constrained Computing

Dharti is technologically advanced but power-constrained, with very little surplus energy. Cloud-scale computing is rare and expensive because of its energy demand, and AI is generally understood as a theoretical concept while practical progress toward advanced AI has been minimal — there is simply not enough sustainable surplus power to sustain large-scale compute. This is why Mara's nuclear transition is expected to dramatically shift global geopolitics, and why Echo matters so much: Ravi's approach enables a power-efficient form of digital consciousness in an energy-constrained civilisation, making her both a singular anomaly and a coveted prize.

**Relationships:** baseline-of → dharti · anomaly-within → echo

# Equatorial Ring Telecom Backbone

Before satellites, Dharti's long-distance telecommunications rely on an equatorial ring of undersea and overland backbone lines, supported by maintenance waystations, cable landing sites, and high-altitude relay infrastructure. The ring topology provides redundancy by allowing data to route in either direction around the planet. It is the planetary nervous system of the pre-satellite era, later extended (and partly superseded) when Mara launches the first man-made satellites.

### Ground-Effect Container Lifter
<sub>also: Wing-in-ground-effect lifter · status: locked</sub>

# Ground-Effect Container Lifter

A wing-in-ground-effect freight craft carrying a baseline payload of 10 standard 20-foot containers (10 TEU), with a route baseline of Kenya to Sri Lanka in a single straight-line over-water transit. It uses an assisted sled launch at the port of origin so onboard energy is not consumed for take-off, and it operates strictly in ground effect over the ocean surface — it cannot safely climb to high altitude or deviate far from its planned corridor. Power comes from upper-surface solar arrays plus a structural-battery superstructure integrated into the wingbox and central fuselage (approximately three times Earth lithium-ion energy density). Visually, a heavy dark modular battery superstructure forms the spine and ribs, with lighter alumelium skins as a brighter outer layer.

**Relationships:** powered-by → structural-batteries · freight-of → dharti

### Hovercraft-Maglev Freight System
<sub>status: locked</sub>

# Hovercraft-Maglev Freight System

Bandarpur's mode-switching transport system, designed for an island chain with frequent landfall. On land and stable island segments the consist couples to energised maglev rails and uses electromagnetic propulsion, drawing power from the track; across open-water gaps each module rides on a hovercraft skirt, with lift and thrust from enclosed fans and ducted impellers integrated into the module body. A dedicated engine carriage houses the primary structural-battery superstructure and power electronics, freeing freight carriages for cargo. It handles up to roughly 100 km of open water between rail endpoints and recharges on the maglev network, with the core design goal being a seamless transition at shoreline terminals between hover and maglev modes without disassembly. Open-water legs are hover corridors, never across-water rail.

**Relationships:** serves → bandarpur · powered-by → structural-batteries
